title: Generative AI Strategy and Productivity Assessment Framework for Life Sciences
summary: Framework for evaluating and deploying generative AI capabilities across life sciences operations, including a 5-level complexity model, cost-benefit assessment approach, and architectural patterns for enterprise AI platforms.

findings.five_level_complexity_model: AI use cases are classified by implementation complexity: Level 1 (basic chatbot — general Q&A with off-the-shelf LLMs), Level 2 (domain chatbot — RAG over internal knowledge bases), Level 3 (workflow assistant — multi-step task automation with tool use), Level 4 (specialized agent — domain-trained models with custom fine-tuning), Level 5 (complex bespoke — multi-agent orchestration with proprietary data pipelines and compliance guardrails).
findings.cost_benefit_assessment: Each level has different cost profiles: Level 1-2 use API-based pricing with minimal infrastructure; Level 3-4 require dedicated compute, retrieval infrastructure, and prompt engineering investment; Level 5 requires ML engineering teams, training infrastructure, and ongoing model maintenance. ROI increases with level but so does risk and time-to-value.
findings.enterprise_architecture_patterns: Common patterns for enterprise AI deployment: (a) API gateway with model routing for multi-provider flexibility, (b) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with vector databases for domain knowledge, (c) Kubernetes-based serving infrastructure for model hosting, (d) observability pipelines for prompt/response monitoring and compliance logging.
findings.life_sciences_specific_considerations: Pharma-specific requirements include: GxP compliance for any AI output used in regulated decisions, audit trails for AI-assisted content generation, validated system requirements for clinical-facing applications, and data residency constraints for models processing patient or HCP data.
findings.productivity_gains_observed: Early adopters report 20-40% productivity gains in: medical writing (first drafts), regulatory document assembly, field medical insight summarization, and internal IT support. Gains are highest in structured, repetitive tasks with clear quality benchmarks.
findings.organizational_readiness: Successful AI adoption requires: executive sponsorship with clear use case prioritization, a center of excellence or AI guild for knowledge sharing, data governance foundations (data catalog, access controls, quality standards), and change management for workflow integration.

source: Consolidated from generative AI strategy presentations and productivity assessment frameworks for life sciences internal use cases
